{{Short description|Prime number one less or more than a factorial}}
{{distinguish|primorial}}
{{Infobox integer sequence
| terms_number       = 53
| con_number         = Infinite
| parentsequence     = ''n''!&nbsp;±&thinsp;1
| first_terms        = 2, 3, 5, 7, 23, 719, 5039, 39916801, 479001599, 87178291199
| largest_known_term = 632760!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1
| OEIS               = A088054
}}
A '''factorial prime''' is a [[prime number]] that is one less or one more than a [[factorial]] (all factorials greater than 1 are [[parity (mathematics)|even]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FactorialPrime.html |title=Weisstein, Eric W. "Factorial Prime." From MathWorld}}</ref>

The first 10 factorial primes (for ''n'' = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14) are {{OEIS|id=A088054}}:
:[[2 (number)|2]] (0!&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 or 1!&nbsp;+&nbsp;1), [[3 (number)|3]] (2!&nbsp;+&nbsp;1), [[5 (number)|5]] (3!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), [[7 (number)|7]] (3!&nbsp;+&nbsp;1), [[23 (number)|23]] (4!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), 719 (6!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), 5039 (7!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), 39916801 (11!&nbsp;+&nbsp;1), 479001599 (12!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), 87178291199 (14!&nbsp;−&nbsp;1), ...

''n''!&nbsp;−&thinsp;1 is prime for {{OEIS|id=A002982}}:
:''n'' = 3, 4, 6, 7, 12, 14, 30, 32, 33, 38, 94, 166, 324, 379, 469, 546, 974, 1963, 3507, 3610, 6917, 21480, 34790, 94550, 103040, 147855, 208003, 632760.<ref>{{Cite web
 | last = Caldwell
 | first = Chris
 | title = Factorial primes
 | website = The Prime Pages
 | url = https://t5k.org/top20/page.php?id=30
 | access-date = 2025-06-29
}}
</ref> (resulting in 28 factorial primes)

''n''!&nbsp;+&thinsp;1 is prime for {{OEIS|id=A002981}}:
:''n'' = 0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 27, 37, 41, 73, 77, 116, 154, 320, 340, 399, 427, 872, 1477, 6380, 26951, 110059, 150209, 288465, 308084, 422429. (resulting in 24 unique factorial primes - the prime 2 occurs twice)

No other factorial primes are known {{as of|2025|6|lc=on}}.

When both ''n''!&nbsp;+&thinsp;1 and ''n''!&nbsp;−&thinsp;1 are [[composite number|composite]], there must be at least 2''n''&nbsp;+&thinsp;1 consecutive composite numbers around ''n''!, since besides ''n''!&nbsp;±&thinsp;1 and ''n''! itself, also, each number of form ''n''!&nbsp;±&nbsp;''k'' is [[divisible]] by ''k'' for 2&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''.  However, the necessary length of this gap is asymptotically smaller than the average composite run for [[integer]]s of similar size (see [[prime gap]]).
